transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 mins (rec)
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chu (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connell (Venari CTO), Priya Nair (Venari ML Eng), Marcus Bell (Venari Infra), Sofia (Data Ops)

Summary (auto-gen, maybe imperfect):
Venari is evaluating migration from OpenAI/Anthropic hosted endpoints to Redwood Dedicated. Primary drivers: cost predictability, data residency / VPC needs, eval parity vs current vLLM/TGI self-hosted baseline, and SLA for latency at peak qps. They want to run parity evals on a 3k prompt set and replicate current fine-tuned behavior. Concerns about model compatibility (tokenization, tool-calling parity), KV cache warmup, and how we handle fallbacks to hosted if Dedicated runs out of capacity.

Topics: migration, dedicated vs hosted, vLLM/TGI compatibility, eval parity, SOC2/KMS/VPC, performance benchmarking, pricing

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you taking the time. Quick roll call — I'll hand it to Liam to kick off with what you're hoping to get out of today.
[00:00:10] Liam: Yeah thanks, Samira. We're evaluating moving most generation traffic off OpenAI and some Anthropic calls onto either Redwood Hosted or Dedicated. Main reason cost and compliance. We also run some self-hosted vLLM/TGI experiments for certain models and want parity before switching.
[00:00:30] Ethan: Got it. Can you say rough qps and token mix so we can size Dedicated?
[00:00:35] Priya: Sure — baseline is ~120 qps across 4 model types, burst to 400 qps for 30-60s windows. Prompts are short-ish — median 120 tokens, responses 180 tokens, but we have a heavy chat workload with repeated contexts. Our monthly token volume is around 1.8B tokens.
[00:00:52] Marcus: Plus we have strict residency: EU data, and all keys need to be customer-managed KMS. Air-gap not required but VPC peering and private networking are mandatory.
[00:01:05] Samira: Okay that helps. Redwood Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS and VPC/private control-plane via our Private offering; Dedicated can be provisioned in EU region. We also have per-route SLOs and routing rules so you can keep sensitive routes on Dedicated and non-sensitive on hosted if you want.
[00:01:25] Liam: How deterministic is inference though? Our engineers worry about eval drift — the model outputs need to match current behavior within tolerance. We fine-tuned some models and have prompt engineering that relies on specific tokenizer behavior.
[00:01:40] Ethan: Right — couple things here. First, our model catalog includes open weights and verified variants; we document tokenization differences. Second, for fine-tunes we support loading customer artifacts and can run eval parity suites. If you send your prompt set we can run head-to-head against your vLLM/TGI baseline and OpenAI to show delta.
[00:02:05] Priya: When you say "verified variants" do you mean Redwood does model surgery or are these vanilla weights? vLLM introduced some kernel-level optimizations that change floating rounding, so sometimes outputs differ slightly.
[00:02:18] Ethan: Most variants are vanilla weights with quantization profiles; our runtime applies optimized kernels at inference. There are cases where kernel selection affects low-prob tokens; we include per-token delta reporting in the eval. For production we recommend locking a model commit and running local tests — and we provide a test tenant for parity checks.
[00:02:40] Sofia: And tooling for prompt metrics? We need to track token counts per route and historic latency distributions.
[00:02:47] Samira: Redwood Console gives token-level cost/latency breakdowns per route and model. You can import your prompts to run evals and tie regressions to specific prompt sets — alerts on quality drift.
[00:02:58] Marcus: Security — SOC2, SSO, audit logs. Can you send SOC2 report and explain retention of logs? We need 365 days of auditability for infra ops.
[00:03:08] Samira: Yes, we'll share the security packet. Dedicated and Private have audit logs, and we support long retention as an add-on. For KMS we integrate with customer-managed keys — you keep control.
[00:03:18] Liam: On the latency question, our p95 needs to be around 150–200ms for short prompts during normal traffic. When you run Dedicated, what are realistic p95s for the model family we're looking at?
[00:03:30] Ethan: For the models you're migrating (we think it's 7B and 13B families from OpenAI/Anthropic), on Dedicated with optimizations we typically see p95s in the 80–180ms range depending on sequence length and batching. If you want strict 150ms p95 with bursts to 400 qps, we'd discuss reserved capacity and burst pool sizing. We'll capture your sequence length distribution and run sizing.
[00:03:53] Priya: About compatibility — tool-calling and function calling semantics differ across runtimes. We rely on a function-call like interface for structured outputs. How do you guarantee behavior?
[00:04:03] Ethan: We support OpenAI-style function call semantics and structured output helpers. We test for behavior during parity runs; if you use a wrapper that relies on specific temperature/sampling configs we'll replicate those. There are edge cases with tokenization and whitespace that can change outputs, we highlight those in the report.
[00:04:20] Liam: We also use vLLM in prod for some models. Are we going to see large differences if we move to Redwood's runtime? vLLM uses continuous batching and some custom caching.
[00:04:30] Samira: Our runtime also does continuous batching, KV cache warmup and prefix caching. Differences come down to kernel-level float ops and quantization. The parity eval will show token-level diffs and a quality metric. If there's a regression beyond your threshold we can test alternate quantization or run at FP16 for that route.
[00:04:50] Marcus: What's the migration path? Do we need to retrain anything or can we just switch endpoints?
[00:04:56] Ethan: Most customers start with a smoke-run in Hosted or a small Dedicated pool and run parity evals. Usually no retrain needed, but sometimes minor prompt adjustments or tokenization normalization reduce diffs. We provide a pre-migration checklist: prompt set export, model version lock, tokenization notes, and integration tests for function calls.
[00:05:15] Priya: About evals — we have a 3k prompt set and an internal BLEU-like metric plus human scoring. Can Redwood ingest that and run automated runs?
[00:05:25] Samira: Yes, we can ingest your prompt set and run automated eval pipelines. We'll return per-prompt diffs, aggregate metrics, and flag items that need human review. It can be integrated in your CI too.
[00:05:36] Liam: Pricing — curious how Dedicated pricing compares to our current OpenAI spend. We pay heavy for embeddings and chat.
[00:05:44] Samira: Dedicated is reserved capacity. We'll share a sample pricing sheet based on your qps and token mix — typically unit token costs drop with Dedicated due to fixed GPU amortization and batching. There's also an extra line for observability retention and premium SLA.
[00:05:58] Marcus: Any hidden engineering lift? Our infra team wants an automated deploy path and IaC.
[00:06:04] Ethan: We have Terraform modules and API-first provisioning; Dedicated capacity provisioning can be automated and we support webhooks for lifecycle events. For Private deployments there's an install bundle for on-prem, but that has a longer lead time.
[00:06:16] Sofia: About fallbacks — if Dedicated is saturated, can we fall back to Hosted?
[00:06:21] Samira: Yes, smart routing supports policy-based fallbacks by route or latency. We can keep a burst buffer on Hosted. You can set cost thresholds per route too.
[00:06:31] Priya: Tokenization specifics — can you confirm which tokenizer versions you use for common open weights? We've seen small differences vectorized by whitespace handling.
[00:06:39] Ethan: We track tokenizer versions in the model catalog; we can lock to a specific tokenizer and share diffs. There are also options to normalize inputs on our SDK side to reduce variance.
[00:06:50] Liam: Ok, sounds promising. A few quick clarifying questions from me: 1) Are we able to bring our own fine-tunes? 2) Will the Dedicated environment allow A/B rollouts? 3) How do you measure quality regressions over time?
[00:07:03] Samira: 1) Yes, BYO fine-tunes — there's a process for onboarding artifacts securely. 2) Yes — rollouts, canary, A/B, and automatic fallback are supported in Redwood Console. 3) We tie evals and prompt sets to alerts: you define thresholds; if quality drops we notify and can auto-roll back.
[00:07:20] Marcus: For the BYO fine-tunes, how are weights stored and who has access?
[00:07:25] Ethan: We use encrypted storage with KMS controls; access is RBACed and we keep audit logs. You can set that keys are customer-managed.
[00:07:33] Priya: A practical question — latency during cold cache vs warm cache. Our use-case has repeated contexts where KV cache matters a lot.
[00:07:41] Ethan: With KV caching warm and prefix caching, tail latency drops significantly. We instrument cache warmup and can show warm vs cold p95 in the benchmark. If your workload has long contexts we recommend specific shard sizing to keep KV hit rate high.
[00:07:56] Liam: Anything else about the eval parity process? I want the run to be reproducible and auditable for our compliance team.
[00:08:02] Samira: We'll provision a test tenant, run three baseline runs (your vLLM/TGI baseline, OpenAI, Redwood Dedicated) and produce a reproducible report with seed settings, tokenizer, model commit, and hardware metadata. That should satisfy audit needs.
[00:08:18] Sofia: On the compliance side we may need an in-person SOC review later; is that something you support?
[00:08:24] Samira: Yes, for enterprise customers we do compliance enablement calls and can share SOC2 artifact and support audits.
[00:08:31] Priya: For the benchmark, will you support TGI specifically? Our in-house stack uses TGI with custom sampling.
[00:08:38] Ethan: We can run TGI-based baselines if you provide config. The parity run will include both greedy and sampling comparisons and report per-metric variance.
[00:08:49] Liam: Great. Let's talk timeline — ideally a pilot in two weeks, full migration in 8–10 weeks if parity checks out.
[00:08:58] Samira: That seems doable. Immediate next steps from Redwood: I'll send the security packet and pricing; Ethan will own the benchmark plan.
[00:09:07] Ethan: I'll put together a benchmark doc with test vectors, hardware assumptions, and a plan to run vLLM and Redwood Dedicated side-by-side.
[00:09:14] Priya: We'll share the 3k prompt set, human scoring rubric, and token metrics.
[00:09:19] Samira: Perfect. Anything else?
[00:09:23] Liam: One more — in case of quality regressions post-migration, what's the rollback model?
[00:09:29] Samira: You can pin traffic back to Hosted or to a previous model commit; rollouts are route-level so rollback is fast. We'll document runbooks in the SOC packet.
[00:09:40] Marcus: Noted. Thanks.
[00:09:43] [crosstalk] Priya: Okay, we'll send artifacts.
[00:09:48] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the packet and pricing by Friday. I'll cc Ethan on the benchmark plan.
[00:09:56] Liam: Thanks, appreciate it.
[00:10:00] END OF RECORDED HIGHLIGHTS — remaining conversation was scheduling details and clarifications (approx 42 mins of Q&A and technical notes omitted here for concision).
